To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
intelligibility is rate-invariant, and that the rate-invariant intelligiblity can be predicted by a measure of relative dissimilarity in cochlear-scaled spectral entropy.

intelligibility of temporaly distorted sentences is rate invariant, and that a cochlea-scaled spectral metric predicts intelligibility better than does a metric based on modulation transfer functions.

In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental question of how the auditory system processes the acoustic speech signal to extract the linguistic content.
the information content of the speech signal and the way that information is extracted by listeners.
the relationship between information and intelligibility, and the relative importance of temporal and spectral cues in speech processing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relative dissimilarity of cochlear scaled spectra, measured as spectral entropy, is a reliable predictor of speech intelligibility, across a range of rates and types of speech distortion.
the relative dissimilarity of successive cochlear-spectra is the best predictor of the intelligibility of temporallly distorted sentences.
the cochlea-scaled spectral information is a more robust and accurate predictor of speech intelligibility than modulation spectrum, which is a more accurate predictor than physical time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relative dissimilarity between successive cochlear spectra predicts speech intelligibility better than any other metric tested.
the information in speech is not rate invariant, but the information in speech can be made rate invariant by using the right metrics.
, in the case of speech intelligibility, the information-theoretic perspective is superior to the physical perspective.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cochlea is the appropriate scale at which to quantify speech information.
the cochlea, rather than the ear, should be the reference point for the study of speech perception.
, in the absence of a time scale, the relative dissimilarity metric is a robust and reliable predictor of speech intelligibility.
